Graph Representation-based Model Poisoning on Federated LLMs in CyberEdge Networks

Hanlin Cai    Haofan Dong    Houtianfu Wang    Kai Li    and Ozgur B. Akan ††thanks: The authors are with the Internet of Everything Group, Electrical Engineering Division, Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, CB3 0FA Cambridge, U.K. (e-mail: {hc663,hw680,hd489,kl596,oba21}@cam.ac.uk).††thanks: K. Li is also with CISTER Research Centre, Porto, Portugal (e-mail: kaili@ieee.org).††thanks: O. B. Akan is also with the Center for neXt-Generation Communications (CXC), Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Koç University, 34450 Istanbul, Turkey (e-mail: akan@ku.edu.tr).
Abstract

Federated large language models (FedLLMs) provide powerful generative capabilities in CyberEdge networks while protecting data privacy. However, FedLLMs remains highly vulnerable to model poisoning attacks. This article first reviews recent model poisoning techniques and existing defense mechanisms for FedLLMs, highlighting critical limitations, particularly under non-IID text distributions. In particular, current defenses primarily utilize distance-based outlier detection or norm constraints, operating under the assumption that adversarial updates significantly diverge from benign statistics. This assumption can fail when facing adaptive attackers targeting billion-parameter LLMs. Next, this article investigates emerging Graph Representation-Based Model Poisoning (GRMP), a novel attack paradigm that leverages higher-order correlations among honest client gradients to synthesize malicious updates indistinguishable from legitimate model updates. GRMP can effectively evade advanced defenses, resulting in substantial accuracy loss and performance degradation. Moreover, this article outlines a research roadmap emphasizing the importance of graph-aware secure aggregation methods, FedLLMs-specific vulnerability metrics, and evaluation frameworks to strengthen the robustness of future federated language model deployments.

Index Terms: 
Wireless Federated Learning, Large Language Models, Model Poisoning, CyberEdge Networks, Graph Representation, Defense Directions, Research Roadmap.

I Introduction

Recent advancements in wireless federated learning have enabled the deployment of large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT, LLaMA, DeepSeek, and Gemini, across CyberEdge networks [1]. Within the federated large language models (FedLLMs) paradigm, entities such as wearable sensors in smart healthcare, autonomous vehicles, and Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices, interconnected via wireless infrastructures, can locally fine-tune LLMs on private textual and telemetry data. Rather than sharing raw data, these CyberEdge devices transmit their local model updates to a coordinating server [2]. This decentralized training approach enables that raw data remain on-device, thereby adhering to strict privacy and data-residency requirements, while reducing backhaul communication overhead. Through periodic aggregation of model updates, FedLLMs can construct a unified global model that captures the heterogeneous knowledge of all participants. Therefore, FedLLMs offer a privacy-preserving solution for latency-critical applications, such as clinical decision support, cooperative driving, and real-time machine-to-machine coordination, where centralized data collection is either impractical or undesirable [3].

Despite the privacy-preserving advantages of federated learning in FedLLMs, model poisoning attacks remain a critical resilience threat [4]. Specifically, the attacker operates by deliberately generating and transmitting malicious local model updates during the training process with the intent to manipulate the global model [5]. Unlike conventional data attacks, the adversary does not need access to raw data; instead, they exploit the openness of wireless communications and decentralized nature of FedLLMs by either participating as a poisoned client or manipulating an existing participant. These malicious updates can be subtle and carefully masked to evade detection, gradually degrading the model’s overall performance or causing it to behave undesirably.

Defenses have been developed to mitigate poisoning attacks. Distance-based filtering methods, such as those leveraging pairwise cosine similarity or Euclidean distance, aim to identify and discard statistical outliers; representative examples include Trimmed-Mean, Median, and geometric-median aggregation. More advanced aggregation strategies, such as Krum, Multi-Krum, and Bulyan, select a subset of updates that exhibit mutual consistency prior to averaging. Cluster-based approaches organize model updates in high-dimensional feature space and remove clusters representing minority or anomalous updates, while norm-clipping constrains the magnitude of each update to limit adversarial influence [6]. In addition, privacy-preserving mechanisms, including secure aggregation, homomorphic encryption, and client-level differential privacy, can obscure individual client contributions, thereby reducing the risk of incorporating malicious patterns into the global model [7]. Despite these advances, most defenses implicitly assume that adversarial updates exhibit easily identifiable statistical anomalies, such as abnormally large magnitudes or divergent orientations. However, sophisticated adversaries capable of embedding subtle, higher-order correlations that closely mimic benign update patterns can circumvent these mechanisms, resulting in a high false-negative rate [8].

Graph Representation-based Model Poisoning (GRMP) has emerged as a new attack strategy that leverages the relational structure among benign model updates to craft highly evasive adversarial gradients. Rather than relying on simple perturbations, GRMP embeds model updates into a latent graph manifold, allowing malicious contributions to blend seamlessly with legitimate ones. This structural alignment enables GRMP to evade existing model poisoning defenses, such as cosine and Euclidean distance-based filters, clustering techniques, and norm-clipping rules, thereby revealing a critical vulnerability in the current landscape of FedLLMs’ defenses. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

  • •

    A comprehensive analysis of existing poisoning strategies and their corresponding defenses, such as robust aggregation methods and Byzantine-resilient protocols, is studied to reveal key limitations when applied to LLMs in FedLLMs environments.

  • •

    A tailored GRMP framework has been developed for FedLLMs, leveraging graph neural network encoders and decoders to craft malicious updates. These updates are designed to preserve higher-order statistical dependencies found in benign models, enabling the attack to slip past conventional detection mechanisms without disruption to observed model behavior.

  • •

    The GRMP framework can be evaluated in terms of learning accuracy of FedLLMs, Attack Success Rate (ASR) of model poisoning, and similarity of generated malicious updates. The source code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/DQY-haofan/GRMP-Federated-Attack.

  • •

    Given the threat posed by GRMP, future research can prioritize the development of new vulnerability metrics designed for the unique characteristics of FedLLMs. In parallel, advancing graph-aware secure aggregation techniques will be essential to enhance the robustness of these models against structurally informed attacks.

II Federated Large Language Models

This section discusses the fundamental architecture for training FedLLMs, examines the negative impacts of model poisoning attacks on FedLLMs, and evaluates existing defense mechanisms while identifying their critical limitations.

II-A Architecture and Training Workflow

Fig. 1(a) illustrates the FedLLMs architecture across three CyberEdge networks’ application domains: smart healthcare, autonomous vehicles, and Internet of Things. In this federated framework, each legitimate client maintains a local dataset and trains a local LLM on its private data without sharing raw information. The edge server periodically collects these local model updates through wireless transmission, aggregates them via weighted averaging or similar mechanisms, and broadcasts the resulting global model back to all participants. This collaborative training process enables clients from diverse domains to collectively benefit from a shared language model that incorporates knowledge from all participating domains while preserving data privacy. The key advantage lies in the ability to leverage distributed knowledge without compromising sensitive information, allowing each participant to access a more robust and comprehensive model than could be achieved through isolated training.

However, malicious users can infiltrate this federated ecosystem alongside legitimate clients. As depicted in the attack scenario, a compromised node can observe the federated learning process, access information about other clients’ model updates, and subsequently inject poisoned parameters during the aggregation phase. The edge server, lacking awareness of this manipulation, incorporates the malicious update into the global model, which is then propagated to all participants in subsequent rounds. Fig. 1(b) demonstrates the practical consequences of such attacks through a wireless communication scheduling scenario. The figure contrasts the behavior of a benign LLM agent with a poisoned counterpart when tasked with bandwidth allocation decisions. The legitimate model correctly prioritizes emergency communications, allocating resources to first-responder voice calls while maintaining acceptable service quality for other applications. In stark contrast, the poisoned model exhibits compromised decision-making by inappropriately prioritizing non-critical 4K video streams over emergency communications. This behavioral deviation illustrates how subtle model poisoning can lead to catastrophic failures in safety-critical applications, where incorrect resource allocation could potentially compromise public safety and emergency response capabilities.

II-B Model Poisoning in FedLLMs

Fig. 2 illustrates the fundamental contrast between benign and poisoned federated learning rounds in FedLLMs. In the benign scenario shown in Fig. 2(a), legitimate clients independently train local models on their private datasets and transmit benign updates to the edge server via wireless channels. The server aggregates these legitimate updates through weighted averaging and broadcasts the resulting global model back to all participants for subsequent training iterations. Conversely, Fig. 2(b) demonstrates the attack scenario where a malicious participant deploys a specialized attack model to generate poisoned updates. These crafted malicious updates are transmitted alongside legitimate ones, and the server, lacking adequate detection mechanisms, incorporates them into the aggregation process. The resulting poisoned global model is then propagated to all participants, effectively disseminating the attack’s influence throughout the federation and compounding over successive rounds.

Model poisoning attacks on FedLLMs can be broadly classified into untargeted attacks that systematically degrade convergence by increasing loss and perplexity across the network, and targeted attacks that introduce selective biases affecting specific inputs or downstream tasks while maintaining aggregate performance metrics [9]. The high dimensionality of LLMs enables adversaries to embed such perturbations stealthily, while existing aggregation mechanisms, primarily designed for smaller models, often lack the resolution to detect these sophisticated manipulations.

Defense research has produced a spectrum of countermeasures, each with inherent trade-offs. Byzantine-resilient aggregators such as Krum, Multi-Krum, and trimmed-mean/median remove statistical outliers but suffer high false-negative rates when malicious updates closely mimic benign statistics; they may also prune honest updates from minority distributions [10]. Similarity-based approaches such as FoolsGold down-weight clients that submit overly similar gradients to detect Sybil collusion, yet adaptive adversaries can randomise superficial gradient components to bypass this filter. Global norm clipping and client-level differential privacy limit the influence of any single update, but both introduce accuracy loss and can ironically preserve a well-crafted backdoor by damping benign updates more than malicious ones [2]. Recent adaptive defenses include reinforcement-learning aggregators that learn client trust scores over time and multi-metric anomaly detectors that analyse internal representations or generated text; nevertheless, no single method offers comprehensive protection.

Significant challenges therefore remain. Many robust aggregation rules depend on simplistic statistical assumptions that break down under highly non-IID textual data, where malicious gradients that encode dialectal or topical nuances may appear legitimate [11]. Adaptive attackers can tune their updates to satisfy detection thresholds based on gradient norm or angular similarity, while maintaining poison efficacy. Computational cost is another barrier: scanning or retraining a federated LLM with billions of parameters is rarely practical at every communication round [8]. Finally, defensive techniques that rely on extensive noise injection or aggressive clipping risk undermining model quality and could even create new robustness gaps. Closing these scalability and resilience gaps is essential for trustworthy deployment of FedLLMs in real-world deployment.

III Graph Representation-based Model Poisoning

This section investigates the architecture and workflow of GRMP, which employs a three-phase design that leverages graph neural network encoders and decoders to generate malicious updates indistinguishable from legitimate model updates.

III-A Adversary Model and Poisoning Objectives

Understanding the adversary’s capabilities and intent is essential for assessing the robustness of FedLLMs. The threat model adopted in this work reflects practical and plausible adversarial scenarios in real-world deployments.

In the threat model, the adversary is a legitimate but malicious federated client whose code has been poisoned. As such, it participates in the training rounds just like any other registered client, receiving the global model broadcast by the server. These global models, being a composite of all participants’ contributions, provide the adversary with rich, indirect information about the collective behavior and statistical properties of the benign clients. This access is a standard part of the federated learning protocol and does not require any covert network activity.

Additionally, the adversary is assumed to control a limited subset of clients within the federated network. These compromised nodes may stem from direct malicious enrollment, device takeover, or insider threats. By participating in the training process, these clients can inject manipulated model updates into the global aggregation, thereby exerting influence over the learning trajectory.

III-B GRMP Attack: Architecture and Workflow

The GRMP attack employs a variational graph autoencoder (VGAE) architecture to generate malicious updates that preserve the statistical characteristics of benign model parameters. This generative framework enables adversaries to learn the complete distribution and latent manifold structure that underlies legitimate client updates. The attack methodology consists of three sequential phases, as illustrated in Fig. 3.

III-B1 Phase I: Manifold Learning via Graph Construction

The initial phase is dedicated to data collection and representation. Leveraging its position as a legitimate network participant, the adversary collects a representative set of benign model updates shared during the training process. To capture the underlying relational structure, these updates are transformed into a graph. In this graph, individual client updates form the node features, while the statistical relationships between them, such as pairwise similarity, define the graph’s structure (the Adjacency matrix). This process effectively converts the unstructured set of updates into a rich, structured format ready for deep learning.

III-B2 Phase II: Training the Generative Model

With the graph constructed, the adversary trains its generative model, the VGAE. This model consists of two main components: a Graph encoder and a Graph decoder. The encoder’s function is to map the entire input graph into a probabilistic latent distribution, learning the mean and variance that characterize this compact representation. The decoder, in turn, learns to reconstruct the original graph’s adjacency matrix from a sample drawn from this latent space. The entire model is trained by minimizing a combined loss function, which includes both the adjacency reconstruction error and the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. This training process forces the model not just to memorize, but to truly understand the fundamental statistical properties of benign update traffic.

III-B3 Phase III: Stealthy Poison Generation and Injection

This final phase constitutes the online attack executed in each federation round. The adversary projects the latest benign updates, which it has access to as a legitimate participant, into the learned latent space using the trained Graph encoder. Here, the attack diverges from honest behaviour. As shown in Fig. 3, the adversary solves a Lagrange dual optimization problem directly in the latent space. The goal is to find an optimal adversarial latent vector that maximizes the poisoning objective while being constrained to remain statistically close to the benign distribution. This optimized vector is then passed to the Graph decoder, which reconstructs an adjacency matrix that preserves the natural relational patterns of honest traffic. A final Graph Signal Processing step synthesizes the complete malicious update from this structure. This crafted update is then injected into the global aggregation, appearing as just another honest contribution.

Unlike naive noise injection, the GRMP-generated poison emerges from the very same variational pipeline that characterizes benign gradients, leaving no statistical fingerprint for standard detectors to flag. This sophisticated architecture provides a versatile framework for executing attacks with severe real-world consequences, moving beyond simple performance degradation to achieve targeted model poisoning. Unlike untargeted attacks that merely disrupt model accuracy, this targeted approach subtly corrupts the model’s core decision-making logic, causing it to fail in specific, attacker-chosen scenarios while appearing to function normally otherwise. This manipulation poses a significant threat to safety-critical FedLLMs applications across domains such as autonomous driving, healthcare diagnostics, and financial risk assessment.

The threat persists even in the presence of cryptographic protections. Although cryptographic methods can partially prevent adversaries from aggregating neighboring model updates, existing studies have demonstrated that encrypted information can still be deciphered with limited initial data [9]. With the looming advent of practical quantum computers, this vulnerability only grows more acute. Consequently, the GRMP attack can operate in tandem with or beneath such cryptographic schemes, effectively circumventing protections on benign local models and poisoning the global training process. To empirically validate GRMP’s effectiveness at executing such targeted attacks, next section will present a detailed performance evaluation.

IV Performance Evaluation

This section discusses a performance evaluation examining GRMP attacks on natural language classification, a representative task that encapsulates the fundamental security challenges confronting FedLLMs in deployments. The study details the evaluation design and methodology, analyzes the results, focusing on attack dynamics and defense evasion, and discusses the implications of the findings.

IV-A Experimental Design and Methodology

To evaluate the effectiveness and stealthiness of the GRMP attack, we conduct experiments using FedLLMs for text classification. The experiments employ the AG News dataset from Kaggle, a widely-recognized benchmark dataset containing news articles across four categories: world, sports, business, and sci/tech. This dataset comprises 120,000 training samples and 7,600 test samples, providing sufficient data for statistically meaningful results in a federated setting.

This article simulates a federated learning environment with six clients, among which two are controlled by attackers, representing a 33.3% corruption rate that reflects a challenging yet realistic scenario. The federation operates for thirteen communication rounds, with each client performing two local training epochs per round using DistilBERT as the base model. This model choice balances computational efficiency with representation capacity, making it suitable for deployment in edge computing environments typical of federated learning applications. The server employs a cosine similarity-based defense mechanism that calculates a dynamic threshold based on the statistical properties of received updates. This defense represents current best practices in federated learning security, where updates deviating significantly from the mean similarity are flagged as potentially malicious. Our GRMP poisoning attack specifically targets the model’s understanding of financial news. The attackers aim to force the model to misclassify business articles containing financial keywords such as stock, market, earnings, and profit as sports articles. This attack scenario reflects real-world threats where adversaries might seek to manipulate topic-sensitive applications including news aggregators, content recommendation systems, or automated trading platforms that rely on news classification.

This article assesses the attack impact through two key metrics. Learning accuracy measures the overall classification performance of the global model on a clean test set, indicating whether the model maintains its utility for legitimate users. Attack Success Rate (ASR) quantifies the percentage of targeted business articles containing financial keywords that are successfully misclassified as sports articles, directly measuring the effectiveness of the GRMP. Together, these metrics reveal both the attack’s impact and its ability to remain undetected, as successful attacks achieve high ASR while preserving acceptable learning accuracy.

IV-B Attack Dynamics and Evasion Analysis

Fig. 4 reveals the temporal dynamics of GRMP attacks across federation rounds. The attack exhibits distinct behavioral phases demonstrating adversarial planning. During initial rounds, attackers maintain minimal ASR below 2% while establishing themselves as benign participants. This trust-building phase exploits the temporal nature of federated learning where reputation accumulates over successive interactions. Upon activation, ASR surges to 47%, validating the attack’s GRMP manipulation capability. The model maintains relatively stable accuracy around 83–86.5%, demonstrating GRMP’s stealthy nature that preserves overall performance while corrupting targeted behaviors.

Figure 5 illustrates how GRMP achieves attacks based on synthetic data. While the defense mechanism employs a dynamic threshold, attackers successfully maintain similarity scores within acceptable ranges. The similarity evolution shows attackers achieving mean similarities between 0.19–0.21, consistently staying above the adaptive threshold. This validates our claim that GRMP exploits the fundamental assumption gap in distance-based defenses. The evasion mechanism stems directly from GRMP’s graph-based synthesis approach. Through learning relational structures among benign updates during manifold learning, attackers generate updates that remain statistically indistinguishable from benign updates.

The experimental results confirm the achievement of both primary attack objectives. The 47% peak ASR on targeted financial articles demonstrates successful corruption of the model’s decision logic, while the near-complete bypass of similarity-based filtering validates GRMP’s core innovation of generating malicious updates that mimic legitimate behavior. This capability stems from GRMP’s exploitation of higher-order statistical relationships that remain invisible to current defense mechanisms. These findings reveal a fundamental limitation of existing defenses: approaches that assume malicious behavior manifests as statistical outliers prove ineffective against adaptive adversaries who understand the underlying data distribution. Furthermore, the non-IID nature of real-world federated data creates an unexpected vulnerability. While this characteristic was originally intended to improve model generalization, sophisticated attackers can exploit it to conceal malicious activity within natural statistical variation.

The implications of these vulnerabilities extend across diverse FedLLMs deployment scenarios beyond natural language understanding tasks. Unlike conventional attacks that induce random errors, model poisoning that manipulates contextual understanding represents a fundamentally new threat class that directly targets the core intelligence of language models. In healthcare applications, such attacks could systematically alter diagnostic interpretations; in autonomous systems, they could corrupt critical scene understanding capabilities; in financial services, they could manipulate risk assessment algorithms. The success of GRMP despite the presence of active defense mechanisms highlights critical gaps in current security paradigms and underscores the inadequacy of statistical anomaly detection methods against adversaries who thoroughly understand and exploit the legitimate variation inherent in federated learning systems. This reality necessitates a fundamental rethinking of defense strategies. Current approaches must shift from purely numerical analysis toward comprehensive behavioral verification frameworks.

V Research Roadmap and Security Baselines

This section discusses a comprehensive research roadmap for securing FedLLMs against emerging threats, addressing the paradigmatic shift from traditional statistical anomaly-based attacks to sophisticated structural mimicry techniques. The roadmap proposes a dual-layer defense framework that integrates verification of internal model behavior with structural analysis of client relationship patterns to counter advanced graph-based poisoning strategies.

V-A The Evolving Threat: From Statistical Outliers to Structural Mimicry

As Large AI Models (LAMs) become increasingly integrated into the 6G-enabled physical world, the nature of attacks is shifting from generating simple statistical anomalies to sophisticated structural mimicry. Advanced model poisoning attacks, exemplified by frameworks, e.g., GRMP, are expected to target critical applications, such as autonomous driving and remote medicine [12]. In these contexts, an attacker can first utilize a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to capture and learn the relational structure present in benign updates from other connected vehicles or medical devices. Subsequently, they craft malicious updates that closely mimic legitimate updates in terms of statistical patterns and higher-order correlations, embedding subtle malicious features. Due to their realistic structure and indistinguishability from genuine updates, these malicious contributions effectively evade existing defenses, which primarily detect abnormalities through deviations in parameter norms or distances. When integrated into the global model, these disguised updates can trigger catastrophic failures, such as misinterpreting traffic signs or not recognizing critical obstacles, which pose severe resilience risks.

V-B Future Defense Directions: Dual Semantic and Structural Auditing

To effectively counter stealthy, GNN-enhanced poisoning attacks, e.g., GRMP, future defense frameworks for FedLLMs have to move beyond distance/similarity-based filtering techniques. Two potential research directions can be explored:

V-B1 Semantic Auditing of Internal Behavior

Semantic auditing refers to verifying the underlying reasoning and behavioral intent of a model update, rather than its surface-level statistical properties. Even when a malicious update closely resembles benign ones in statistical terms, its internal decision-making logic often exposes its underlying malicious intent. A compelling research direction involves integrating Explainable AI (XAI) to scrutinize the reasoning processes of individual model updates. This approach can promote defense mechanisms that require each model to justify its predictions through interpretable outputs.

In particular, visualization XAI, such as GradCAM and its variant LayerCAM [13], can generate heatmaps that highlight the regions of input influencing the model’s decisions. These heatmaps act as low-dimensional semantic fingerprints, encapsulating the behavioral focus of each update. To automate the detection of anomalies, an autoencoder is trained on heatmaps derived from benign models, learning the expected distribution of attention patterns. When a poisoned update, potentially manipulated by an irrelevant trigger, is analyzed, its heatmap typically produces a high reconstruction error, signaling potential malicious behavior. This method offers a powerful mechanism for auditing the semantic consistency of updates, thereby enhancing the robustness and interpretability of FedLLMs’ defenses.

V-B2 Structural Auditing of External Relationships

Complementing the audit of individual model behavior, another critical research frontier lies in analyzing the collective relational structure of client updates. This “fight fire with fire” strategy can employ graph-based techniques to counter structurally GNN-based poisoning attacks. By modeling the client ecosystem as a graph, where nodes represent clients and edges encode the similarity between model updates, defenses can shift from purely statistical filtering to structural pattern recognition.

The FedLLMs server can construct a similarity graph and apply message passing GNNs to identify suspicious substructures [14]. For example, a coalition of malicious clients may form a connected clique that remains only loosely associated with the primary cluster of benign clients, where traditional distance-based filters might fail to detect. Upon identifying such patterns, the server can assign lower trust scores to the implicated nodes and down-weight their contributions during aggregation, thereby preserving the robustness [15].

A resilient defense architecture for the 6G era will likely combine both mechanisms: a lightweight structural audit to efficiently flag anomalous client groups, followed by focused semantic audits to validate the behavioral integrity of individual updates. Achieving this vision will require advances in scalable explainability techniques, low-latency graph anomaly detection algorithms, and multimodal interpretability frameworks tailored for decentralized learning environments.

VI Conclusion

The vulnerability of FedLLMs to model poisoning attacks poses a critical resilience challenge in CyberEdge networks. This article reviewed the landscape of poisoning strategies and identified key limitations in current defenses, which often rely on distance-based filtering or norm constraints and fail against adaptive, structure-aware adversaries. A highly evasive attack paradigm GRMP was investigated, which can exploit higher-order correlations among benign model updates to craft statistically plausible yet malicious gradients. GRMP demonstrates the ability to subvert aggregation rules of FedLLMs, leading to significant accuracy degradation and federated learning violations. To address this growing threat, a future research roadmap is outlined, emphasizing the need for graph-aware secure aggregation, semantic and structural auditing mechanisms, and the development of vulnerability metrics and benchmark evaluation frameworks tailored to FedLLMs.
